notes.text: Lord — The eternal word, Jehovah, the same who spake from Mount Sinai. Answered - Out of a dark and thick cloud, from which he sent a tempestuous wind, as the harbinger of his presence. In this manner God appears and speaks to awaken Job and his friends, to the more serious attention to his words; and to testify his displeasure both against Job, and them, that all of them might be more deeply humbled and prepared to receive, and retain the instructions which God was about to give them.

Counsel — God's counsel. For the great matter of the dispute between Job and his friends, was concerning God's counsel and providence in afflicting Job; which Job had endeavoured to obscure and misrepresent. This first word which God spoke, struck Job to the heart. This he repeats and echoes to, chap. xlii, 3, as the arrow that stuck fast in him.
Gird up — As warriors then did for the battle.
Where — Thou art but of yesterday; and dost thou presume to judge of my eternal counsels! When - When I settled it as firm upon its own center as if it had been built upon the surest foundations.
Measures — Who hath prescribed how long and broad and deep it should be. Line - the measuring line to regulate all its dimensions.

Foundations — This strong and durable building hath no foundations but God's power, which hath marvelously established it upon itself. Cornerstone - By which the several walls are joined and fastened together, and in which, next to the foundations, the stability of a building consists. The sense is, who was it that built this goodly fabrick, and established it so firmly that it cannot be moved.

Stars — The angels, who may well be called morning-stars, because of their excellent lustre and glory. Sons of God - The angels called the sons of God, because they had their whole being from him, and because they were made partakers of his Divine and glorious image. Shouted - Rejoiced in and blessed God for his works, whereby he intimates, that they neither did advise or any way assist him, nor dislike or censure any of his works, as Job had presumed to do.
Light — With that first created light, which the psalmist fitly puts in the first place, as being the first of God's visible works.
Waters — In the waters above the heavens, as they are called, Gen. i, 7.

Spirits — Of a spiritual or incorporeal nature, that they might be fitter for their employments. Fire - So called for their irresistible force and agility, and fervency in the execution of God's commands.

Who laid — Hebrew. he hath established the earth upon its own basis, whereby it stands as fast and unmoveable, as if it were built upon the strongest foundations. Forever - As long as the world continues. God has fixt so strange a place for the earth, that being an heavy body, one would think it should fall every moment. And yet which way so ever we would imagine it to stir, it must, contrary to the nature of such a body, fall upwards, and so can have no possible ruin, but by tumbling into heaven.
The deep — In the first creation, Gen. i, 2, 9.
Rebuke — Upon thy command, Gen. i, 9. Fled - They immediately went to the place which God had allotted them.
Go up — In that first division of the waters from the earth, part went upwards, and became springs in the mountains, the greatest part went downwards to the channels made for them.
A bound — Even the sand of the sea-shore.

glossa.text: *A psalm of David.* ((CASS.)) Likewise God *Deus*; read *Deum*, "to bless God" admonishes men to bless, first through heaven and earth and their adornment. ((AUG.)) Although indeed all things here may be devoutly taken according to the letter, etc., *as far as* in all things the spiritual sense is to be sought. *Bless the Lord, O my soul,* etc., *magnified.* *mugnificatus* In knowledge, because thou art always great by nature, who thinkest *putes*; read *potes*, "thou canst" not to grow or be lessened, because thou art perfect; *Confession,* that is, thou hast on every side creatures which confess thee, and which are comely and full of light. Or, comeliness is in the essence of God, and light on every side. ((CASS.)) Or it signifies the incarnation, through which the confession and the glory of the heavenly majesty became known, and men confessed him, who are light by knowledge. ((AUG.)) Thou hast put on confession, that is, the Church, etc., *as far as* and a garment without spot or wrinkle.

*Stretching out the heaven thus.* ((CASS.)) What things confess him? Heaven, earth, sea, with all their adornment; of each of these in what follows. ((AUG.)) *Stretching out the heaven like.* According to the letter, the heaven, as it were a roof, etc., *as far as* afterwards at the end, like a book, Scripture shall be folded up.

*Who coverest.* ((ID.)) According to the letter they are waters, etc., *as far as* whose upper parts are the two precepts of charity. Or thou who *coverest with waters,* that is, with the spiritual sense, the surface of Scripture; or by spiritual gifts thou fortifiest their charity, that nothing may be able to separate them. *Upon the wings of the winds,* etc. Wind is a movement of the air, etc., *as far as* but the charity of Christ surpasses the charity of all.
*A burning fire.* ((CASS.)) That is, the seraphim, who are the higher order, thou makest thy ministers, whence in Isaiah: *There flew to me one of the seraphim,* who are the higher order.
*Who hast founded the earth upon its own stability.* ((ID.)) Therefore the Holy Spirit in this psalm speaks things difficult according to the letter, that we may seek spiritual things.
*At the voice of thunder.* ((ID.)) By terrible winds the waters shall be dried up; the wicked shall fear at the threatening of the judgment.

*They ascend.* ((AUG.)) The wicked, as mountains, etc., *as far as* that the Church may be free to preach. ((CASS.)) God permits the proud, etc., *as far as* that they may no longer take possession of the world.

notes.text: For every high priest being taken from among men — Is, till he is taken, of the same rank with them. And is appointed - That is, is wont to be appointed. In things pertaining to God - To bring God near to men, and men to God. That he may offer both gifts - Out of things inanimate, and animal sacrifices.

Who can have compassion — In proportion to the offense: so the Greek word signifies. On the ignorant - Them that are in error. And the wandering - Them that are in sin. Seeing himself also is compassed with infirmity - Even with sinful infirmity; and so needs the compassion which he shows to others.

The apostle begins here to treat of the priesthood of Christ. The sum of what he observes concerning it is, Whatever is excellent in the Levitical priesthood is in Christ, and in a more eminent manner; and whatever is wanting in those priests is in him. And no one taketh this honour — The priesthood. To himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron - And his posterity, who were all of them called at one and the same time. But it is observable, Aaron did not preach at all; preaching being no part of the priestly office.

So also Christ glorified not himself to be an high priest — That is, did not take this honour to himself, but received it from him who said, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee - Not, indeed, at the same time; for his generation was from eternity. Psalm ii, 7.
Psalm cx, 4.

The sum of the things treated of in the seventh and following chapters is contained, ver. 7-10; and in this sum is admirably comprised the process of his passion, with its inmost causes, in the very terms used by the evangelists. Who in the days of his flesh — Those two days, in particular, wherein his sufferings were at the height. Having offered up prayers and supplications - Thrice. With strong crying and tears - In the garden. To him that was able to save him from death - Which yet he endured, in obedience to the will of his Father. And being heard in that which he particularly feared - When the cup was offered him first, there was set before him that horrible image of a painful, shameful, accursed death, which moved him to pray conditionally against it: for, if he had desired it, his heavenly Father would have sent him more than twelve legions of angels to have delivered him. But what he most exceedingly feared was the weight of infinite justice; the being "bruised" and "put to grief" by the hand of God himself. Compared with this, everything else was a mere nothing; and yet, so greatly did he ever thirst to be obedient to the righteous will of his Father, and to "lay down" even "his life for the sheep," that he vehemently longed to be baptized with this baptism, Luke xii, 50. Indeed, his human nature needed the support of Omnipotence; and for this he sent up strong crying and tears: but, throughout his whole life, he showed that it was not the sufferings he was to undergo, but the dishonour that sin had done to so holy a God, that grieved his spotless soul. The consideration of its being the will of God tempered his fear, and afterwards swallowed it up; and he was heard not so that the cup should pass away, but so that he drank it without any fear.

Though he were a Son — This is interposed. lest any should be offended at all these instances of human weakness. In the garden, how frequently did he call God his Father! Matt. xxvi, 39, &c. And hence it most evidently appears that his being the Son of God did not arise merely from his resurrection. Yet learned he - The word learned, premised to the word suffered, elegantly shows how willingly he learned. He learned obedience, when be began to suffer; when he applied himself to drink that cup: obedience in suffering and dying.

And being perfected — By sufferings, chap. ii, 10; brought through all to glory. He became the author - The procuring and efficient cause. Of eternal salvation to all that obey him - By doing and suffering his whole will.

Called — The Greek word here properly signifies surnamed. His name is, "the Son of God." The Holy Ghost seems to have concealed who Melchisedec was, on purpose that he might be the more eminent type of Christ. This only we know, - that he was a priest, and king of Salem, or Jerusalem.

glossa.text: *For every high priest.* Because spiritual things do not so bring in the weak: as bodily things; from these he begins, wishing to show that the New Testament is better than the Old. But some things he sets down as common to Christ with the priests, some higher, pertaining to Christ alone. Some, further, more lowly, suiting those priests only.
*For that he himself also.* Take away here the occasion of exalting oneself above others.
*Neither doth any man,* etc. He strikes the covetous, who are not called, but thrust themselves forward.

*He did not glorify himself.* The Son was glorified by the Father, when he said: *This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased ((Matth. III))*. Which glorification was foretold long before through the Prophet: *Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee ((Psal. II))*.

*Thou art a priest.* Now Christ is a priest, not according to that whereby he was born of the Father, God with God, coeternal with him that begat him: but on account of the flesh consumed, on account of the victim which he offered for us. *According to the order of Melchisedech,* who was not temporal, Scripture keeping silence as to the beginning and the end of his life, in a figure of Christ who lacks beginning and end. And as he offered in bread and wine and once, so also Christ under the species of bread and wine gave his body and his blood to the disciples.

*Prayers and supplications.* He speaks of the action and the life of Christ, whose every action is the instruction of the faithful, and a prayer to God. Whatever Christ did, they were prayers and supplications for all. The shedding of his blood was a mighty cry, in which he was heard, for the reverence of that same passion. The reverence is this, that being without sin he suffered for charity alone. *He was heard.* By this it is plain that through him we can obtain mercy, since he is now at the right hand of the Father.
*He learned,* etc. That is, he willingly took upon himself obedience even unto death.

*To all that obey him.* So greatly does the passion avail, that it suffices for all unto salvation, which salvation can well be through him, because he himself *is called,* etc. *He was made the cause of salvation,* not of any sort of salvation, but of eternal; nor to few, but to all; yet on this condition, that they obey him. For otherwise they will not be able to obtain salvation. And he himself can well be the cause of salvation to the rest, since *he was called by God a high priest,* as he also himself showed in very deed by his works that he was such. For because he fulfilled the office of a high priest, and was obedient to the Father in all things, and in himself came to so great a consummation of all good things that it sufficed even for the salvation of others, therefore *he was called by God a high priest,* and this, *according to the order of Melchisedech,* namely, that all the order of divinity might be considered in him which could be considered in Melchisedech.

notes.text: Saying — By their mother. It was she, not they that uttered the words. Matt. xx, 20.

Ye know not what ye ask — Ye know not that ye ask for sufferings, which must needs pave the way to glory. The cup - Of inward; the baptism - Of outward sufferings. Our Lord was filled with sufferings within, and covered with them without.

Save to them for whom it is prepared — Them who by patient continuance in well doing, seek for glory, and honour, and immortality. For these only eternal life is prepared. To these, only he will give it in that day; and to every man his own reward, according to his own labour.
A ransom for many — Even for as many souls as needed such a ransom, 2 Cor. v, 15.

glossa.text: *And they come.* Having heard of the resurrection, forgetful of the second coming, they think that he will reign after the manner of men. Matthew says that the mother made the request, but Mark says that they themselves did, wishing to lay open the desire of those by whose counsel the mother asked.
*Or with the baptism.* The same as the cup. Whence elsewhere he says of his passion: *I have a baptism wherewith to be baptized: and how am I straitened until it be accomplished.*

*The cup indeed. ((BED.))* James is beheaded by Herod, John is cast into a cauldron of boiling oil. Thence the athlete of Christ went forth to the crown of martyrdom, and was at once banished to Patmos. And so he both was not wanting to martyrdom in mind, and drank the cup of confession which the three children drank in the furnace, although the persecutor did not shed his blood.

*But to sit.* As if to say, Do you wish that I should grant this to you? But the kingdom of heaven is not the giver's but the receiver's. *For there is no respect of persons with God ((Act. X))*, but whosoever shall be worthy shall receive that which is prepared not for the person but for the life. *To you.* Still proud, as if he said: If you wish to receive, be not what you are: it is prepared for others, and be you others, and it is prepared for you, which is, be humbled first, you who already wish to be exalted.
*They were indignant.* Not about the mother, but about the sons, who, not knowing their own measure, burned with immoderate greed.

*But Jesus calling them.* A humble master, and kind and gentle, he neither reproves the two for immoderate greed nor rebukes the ten for indignation and spite, but teaches that he is the greater who shall have been the less, and lord who is servant. In vain therefore do either those sigh after greater things or these grieve over their desire, since not power but humility leads to the summit of the virtues. Lastly he sets before his own an example, that if they made light of words, they might blush at deeds. *For the Son of man also, etc.*

echoes.text: “Bring Aaron your brother, and his sons with him, near to you from among the children of Israel, that he may minister to me in the priest’s office, even Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron’s sons.
echoes.note: ‘He is called by God, just like Aaron’ (v. 4) names Aaron's installation directly; Exod 28:1 is the foundational text where God ‘brings near’ Aaron to the priesthood. Moderate verbal volume (the proper name Aaron is shared) plus high thematic coherence with the high-priest argument seeded since 2:17 (Hays' recurrence).

echoes.text: to be a memorial to the children of Israel, to the end that no stranger, who isn’t of the offspring of Aaron, would come near to burn incense before Yahweh, that he not be as Korah, and as his company; as Yahweh spoke to him by Moses.
echoes.note: ‘Nobody takes this honor on himself’ (v. 4) recalls the Korah rebellion (Num 16–17), the locus classicus for seizing priesthood uninvited; the bronze-censer memorial of 16:40 warns against the ‘stranger’ who presumes. No verbatim quotation — a thematic allusion to the negative type behind Hebrews' rule of divine calling.

echoes.text: Moses said to Aaron, “Draw near to the altar, and offer your sin offering, and your burnt offering, and make atonement for yourself, and for the people; and offer the offering of the people, and make atonement for them; as Yahweh commanded.”
echoes.note: ‘He must offer sacrifices for sins for the people, as well as for himself’ (v. 3) compresses the cultic logic of Lev 9:7, where Aaron atones first ‘for yourself’ then ‘for the people.’ Verbal coherence (the doubled for-himself/for-the-people structure) marks this as the underlying script; the divergence Hebrews exploits is that Christ, sinless (4:15; 7:27), needs no offering for himself.

echoes.text: “Aaron shall offer the bull of the sin offering, which is for himself, and make atonement for himself and for his house.
echoes.note: The Day-of-Atonement requirement that the high priest atone ‘for himself’ (Lev 16:6) undergirds v. 3 and is the foil Hebrews overturns at 7:27. A faint echo paralleling Lev 9:7; recurrence of the Lev 16 figure already running through the letter (1:3; 9:7) raises its credence (Hays).

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, ‘You are my son. Today I have become your father.’
echoes.note: Re-cited from 1:5, now welded to priesthood: the same divine ‘today’ that enthrones the Son also installs him as high priest. Recurrence binding the two halves of the letter together.

echoes.text: Yahweh has sworn, and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.’
echoes.note: The hinge of the whole letter. Ps 110:1 crowned the Son at 1:13; now verse 4 of the same psalm makes him priest — a priesthood older than Aaron's, sworn by an oath. Named here, expounded at length in chapter 7.

echoes.text: Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine: and he was priest of God Most High.
echoes.note: The name ‘Melchizedek’ (vv. 6, 10) points beyond Ps 110:4 to its narrative root in Gen 14:18, the only other Old Testament Melchizedek text and the one ch. 7 will expound at length. The repeated naming is Hays' recurrence in advance — the figure is planted here and harvested in chapter 7.

echoes.text: For he has not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted, Neither has he hidden his face from him; but when he cried to him, he heard.
echoes.note: ‘Strong crying… having been heard for his godly fear’ (v. 7) reads the righteous sufferer's vindication: the very psalm of the cross (Ps 22, already cited at 2:12) testifies that God ‘heard’ the afflicted one's cry. Thematic coherence and recurrence of Ps 22 in Hebrews make this a heard, if unquoted, link to the Passion.

echoes.text: I love Yahweh, because he listens to my voice, and my cries for mercy. Because he has turned his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live. The cords of death surrounded me, the pains of Sheol got a hold of me. I found trouble and sorrow. Then I called on Yahweh’s name: “Yahweh, I beg you, deliver my soul.”
echoes.note: ‘Prayers and petitions… to him who was able to save him from death, and having been heard’ (v. 7) closely tracks the lament-deliverance pattern of Ps 116: encircled by the ‘cords of death,’ the petitioner cries and is heard. Scholars (Beale & Carson) hear the Gethsemane prayer voiced through the lament psalms; medium volume, strong thematic fit.

echoes.text: “Hear my prayer, Yahweh, and give ear to my cry. Don’t be silent at my tears. For I am a stranger with you, a foreigner, as all my fathers were.
echoes.note: ‘With strong crying and tears’ (v. 7) — the explicit ‘tears’ — faintly echoes the lament topos of Ps 39:12, where the sufferer begs God not to ‘be silent at my tears.’ Low verbal volume and a contested identification (any lament psalm could supply the motif), included for maximal coverage.

echoes.text: You shall not go out from the door of the Tent of Meeting for seven days, until the days of your consecration are fulfilled: for he shall consecrate you seven days.
echoes.note: ‘Having been made perfect’ (teleiōtheis, v. 9) carries the cultic sense of priestly ‘perfecting/consecration’ — the LXX teleioō word-group renders the ‘fill the hand’ ordination of Lev 8 (cf. 8:33, the seven-day consecration). A faint figural link: Christ's perfecting through suffering reworks the priest's installation rite. LXX-specific; invisible in the Hebrew ‘fill the hands.’

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand. After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall […]
echoes.note: The Servant who 'pours out his soul to death,' 'bears the sin of many,' and makes his life a guilt offering 'for many' is the controlling source for 'to give his life as a ransom for many.' The distinctive vicarious 'for many' (rabbim) and the substitutionary death match decisively. This is the chapter's major Servant allusion, high in Volume and Coherence.

echoes.text: Awake, awake, stand up, Jerusalem, that have drunk at the hand of Yahweh the cup of his wrath; you have drunken the bowl of the cup of staggering, and drained it.
echoes.note: Jerusalem has drunk 'the cup of his wrath... the bowl of staggering,' the cup-of-judgment imagery behind 'the cup that I drink.' Jesus takes upon himself the cup of divine wrath the city must drink. The cup as wrath to be consumed coheres with the passion's substitutionary logic.

echoes.text: For in the hand of Yahweh there is a cup, full of foaming wine mixed with spices. He pours it out. Indeed the wicked of the earth drink and drink it to its very dregs.
echoes.note: 'In the hand of the LORD there is a cup... and he pours it out; surely all the wicked of the earth shall drain it' establishes the cup as the draught of God's judgment. Jesus' question 'are you able to drink the cup that I drink' draws on this judicial cup. The wrath-cup motif's Recurrence (Jeremiah 25, Isaiah 51) supports it.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, to me: take this cup of the wine of wrath at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send you, to drink it. They shall drink, and reel back and forth, and be mad, because of the sword that I will send among them. Then took I the cup at Yahweh’s hand, and made all the nations to drink, to whom Yahweh had sent me: Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, and its kings, and its princes, to make them a desolation, an […]
echoes.note: The prophet makes the nations drink 'the cup of the wine of wrath,' the most extended OT development of the wrath-cup that Jesus alludes to. It strengthens the Recurrence of the cup-of-judgment tradition behind Mark 10:38. Marked contested only as to which cup-text is primary; Isaiah 51 and Psalm 75 are nearer.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: James and John request seats 'in your glory,' echoing the dominion and glory given to the son of man, while the right-and-left thrones evoke enthronement in the Danielic kingdom. The petition presupposes the Son of Man's coming glory. Coherence with the Daniel 7 background of Mark's Son of Man title supports the link.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: The request to sit 'at your right hand' draws on the royal enthronement of the king at God's right hand. The right-hand seat of honor is the Psalm 110 image Mark elsewhere applies to Jesus. The single-side request makes the echo partial but apt; marked contested as to directness.

echoes.text: The kingdom and the dominion, and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole sky, shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High: his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.
echoes.note: Dominion is given to the saints, yet the kingdom's authority is from God, against which the Gentile kings who 'lord it over' their nations are contrasted. Jesus' antithesis between Gentile rulers' domination and servanthood draws on this kingdom-of-God-versus-beastly-empires schema. The contrast of empires coheres with Daniel 7.

echoes.text: Seventy weeks are decreed on your people and on your holy city, to finish disobedience, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most holy. Know therefore and discern, that from the going out of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem to the Anointed One, the prince, shall be seven weeks, and sixty-two weeks: it shall be […]
echoes.note: The 'anointed one' cut off and atonement made 'for iniquity' resonates faintly with the ransoming death 'for many.' It supplies a Second-Temple frame for a representative figure's atoning death. Low and contested: conceptual, no verbal lock.

echoes.text: “When you take a census of the children of Israel, according to those who are numbered among them, then each man shall give a ransom for his soul to Yahweh, when you number them; that there be no plague among them when you number them.
echoes.note: The atonement-money 'ransom for his life' paid at the census supplies cultic background for lytron, 'ransom.' It frames a life-price offered to redeem. Contested and low: Mark's ransom is more directly Isaianic (53:10-12), but the redemption-price vocabulary is available here.

echoes.text: after he is sold he may be redeemed. One of his brothers may redeem him; or his uncle, or his uncle’s son, may redeem him, or any who is a close relative to him of his family may redeem him; or if he has grown rich, he may redeem himself.
echoes.note: The kinsman-redeemer who pays a price to redeem (gaal/lytron) supplies the OT economy of ransom behind 'a ransom for many.' It contributes Availability for the redemption metaphor. Contested; background vocabulary rather than citation.

echoes.text: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough,
echoes.note: No one can 'ransom' a brother or give God 'the price of his life,' for the ransom of a soul is costly, sharpening the surprise that the Son of Man does give exactly such a ransom 'for many.' The psalm sets up the impossibility Jesus' death answers. Contested and low: an inverted thematic contact.

notes.text: Yet — Our people believed that he was thus punished by the just judgment of God.

Wounded — Which word comprehends all his pains and punishments. For our iniquities - For the guilt of their sins, which he had voluntarily taken upon himself, and for the expiation of their sins, which was hereby purchased. The chastisement - Those punishments by which our peace, our reconciliation to God, was to be purchased, were laid upon him by God's justice with his own consent. Healed - By his sufferings we are saved from our sins.

We — All mankind. Astray - From God. Have turned - In general, to the way of sin, which may well be called a man's own way, because sin is natural to us, inherent in us, born with us; and in particular, to those several paths, which several men chuse, according to their different opinions, and circumstances. Hath laid - Hebrew. hath made to meet, as all the rivers meet in the sea. The iniquity - Not properly, for he knew no sin; but the punishment of iniquity, as that word is frequently used. That which was due for all the sins of all mankind, which must needs be so heavy a load, that if he had not been God as well as man, he must have sunk under the burden.
He opened not — He neither murmured against God, nor reviled men.

Taken away — Out of this life. By distress and judgment - By oppression and violence. and a pretense of justice. His generation - His posterity. For his death shall not be unfruitful; when he is raised from the dead, he shall have a spiritual seed, a numberless multitude of those who shall believe in him. Cut off - By a violent death. And this may be added as a reason of the blessing of a numerous posterity conferred upon him, because he was willing to be cut off for the transgression of his people.

With the wicked — This was a farther degree of humiliation. He saith, he made his grave, because this was Christ's own act, and he willingly yielded up himself to death and burial. And that which follows, with the wicked, does not denote the sameness of place, as if he should be buried in the same grave with other malefactors, but the sameness of condition.

He — God was the principal cause of all his sufferings, tho' mens sins were the deserving cause. When - When thou, O God, shalt have made, thy son a sacrifice, by giving him up to death for the atonement of mens sins. His soul is here put for his life, or for himself. Shall see - He shall have a numerous issue of believers reconciled by God, and saved by his death. Prolong - He shall live and reign with God forever. The pleasure - God's gracious decree for the salvation of mankind shall be effectually carried on by his ministry and mediation.

Shall see — He shall enjoy. The travel - The blessed fruit of all his labours, and sufferings. Satisfied - He shall esteem his own and his father's glory, and the salvation of his people, an abundant recompence. By his knowledge - By the knowledge of him. Justify - Acquit them from the guilt of their sins, and all the dreadful consequences thereof. And Christ is said to justify sinners meritoriously, because he purchases and procures it for us. Many - An innumerable company of all nations. For - For he shall satisfy the justice of God, by bearing the punishment due to their sins.

I — God the father. A portion - Which is very commodiously supplied out of the next clause. With the strong - God will give him happy success in his glorious undertaking: he shall conquer all his enemies, and set up his universal and everlasting kingdom in the world. Because - Because he willingly laid down his life. Transgressors - He prayed upon earth for all sinners, and particularly for those that crucified him, and in heaven he still intercedes for them, by a legal demand of those good things which he purchased; by the sacrifice of himself, which, though past, he continually represents to his father, as if it were present. The blessings and fulness of the gospel-church, ver. 1-4. The Gentiles becoming Christ's spouse, to whom his love is everlasting, ver. 5-10. Her glories, ver. 11, 12. The gifts of the Holy Ghost, ver. 13. Her sure preservation, ver. 14-17

glossa.text: *By his bruises.* ((ID.)) It is plain that, just as his body was torn and scourged, so his soul truly grieved for us, lest in Christ part be believed truth and part falsehood.

*He opened not,* etc. To Pilate or to Herod. For he answered few things, lest the salvation of the human race be deferred.

*And as a lamb.* ((ID.)) In figure of whom the people of Israel ate the lamb in Egypt ((Exod. XII)). This is the lamb *who taketh away the sins of the world ((Joan. I))*, *who was slain from the beginning of the world ((Apoc. XIII))*, who feeds us with his flesh and his blood, and clothes us with the fleece of his protection.
*From judgment.* The judge of all found no truth of judgment, but was condemned without fault. Whence the prophet marvels that the God of all delivered himself over to the Passion.

*He shall give the wicked.* ((ID.)) That is, the Gentiles, who are without piety, to God the Father, because dead and buried he acquired them; and the rich, namely the Jews, who glory in the riches of the law and of the prophets.

*The rich.* The Scribes and Pharisees, glorying in the riches of the doctrine of the law.
*A long-lived seed.* The word of the Gospel, namely, which shall not grow old, as the Old Testament did, whence: *He that sowed went out to sow his seed ((Luc. VIII.))*

*He shall be filled.* With the faith of the Gentiles, whence, hungering and thirsting above Jacob's well, he would not use the food that had been bought, because he was already filled with the faith of the Samaritan woman and of those who were coming out to him from the city.

*And with the wicked.* That he might redeem the wicked from sin, being made all things to all: *For he bore our sins in his own body ((I Petr. II))*. Whose imitator Paul says: *I became all things to all, that I might gain all ((I Cor. IX))*.

*He prayed.* Father, forgive them. At this voice, according to the Gospel of the Nazarenes, many thousands of the Jews standing about the cross believed.

notes.text: Bear thee — Sustain or uphold thee in thy goings, as we do a child.

The lion — Shall lie prostrate at thy feet, and thou shalt securely put thy feet upon his neck. Dragon - By which he understands all pernicious creatures, though never so strong, and all sorts of enemies.

Because — This and the two following verses are the words of God. God is praised for his works, ver. 1-5. The doom of the wicked, from the eternal God, ver. 6-9. The prosperity of the righteous, ver. 10-15. A psalm or song for the sabbath-day.

glossa.text: *For thou art.* ((AUG.)) One Christ is head and body, of whom he speaks now as of the head, now as of the body, the person not being changed. Therefore diligently mark where he treats of Christ according to the head, and where according to the members. *The Most High.* In the height is the refuge of God, deep in secret, that flight may be made from the wrath to come. For many so make for themselves the refuge of God, whereby they flee from temporal evils. *Thou hast made the Most High thy refuge,* that is, by rising again, by ascending, thou hast made the refuge high, that I may now hope to follow *speram* whither thou hast gone before.
((ID.)) *The tabernacle of God* is the flesh, etc., *as far as* this is rightly taken of Christ.

*For to his angels.* This the tempter said to the Lord, when he tempted him: this he cast up against him, doubting of his Godhead. But Christ was tempted for our sake, that in him also we might learn to overcome the tempter.

((AUG.)) So also he willed to be baptized by a servant, not for his own need, but for man's profit, that we should not disdain to be baptized by our fellow servants.
*In their hands they shall bear thee up.* ((ID.)) By the hands of angels Christ was lifted up into heaven, etc., *as far as* he who cannot be overcome.

*Upon the asp.* After the human infirmity, the divine power is shown, which commands such creatures. And he treats of Christ according to the members. *And he shall trample.* ((AUG.)) The Church, which is wary of his cunning, treads upon the serpent. *The lion.* He rages openly against the martyrs.

The dragon lies in wait through the heretics, that he may corrupt the virgin of Christ, whence the Apostle: *I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you a chaste virgin to Christ ((II Cor. XI))*.

*Because he hoped in me.* ((AUG.)) Thirdly, the words of God, by which he consoles the Church, to which he promises both defence here, and rewards in the world to come. ((CASS.)) He gives charge to the angels concerning thee, saying: *Because in me.* The certainty of the promise, through the promise of God.
*He shall cry to me.* ((AUG.)) There is no need to fear in tribulation, etc., *as far as* at that time let us labour the more to resist.

notes.text: For every high priest being taken from among men — Is, till he is taken, of the same rank with them. And is appointed - That is, is wont to be appointed. In things pertaining to God - To bring God near to men, and men to God. That he may offer both gifts - Out of things inanimate, and animal sacrifices.

Who can have compassion — In proportion to the offense: so the Greek word signifies. On the ignorant - Them that are in error. And the wandering - Them that are in sin. Seeing himself also is compassed with infirmity - Even with sinful infirmity; and so needs the compassion which he shows to others.

The apostle begins here to treat of the priesthood of Christ. The sum of what he observes concerning it is, Whatever is excellent in the Levitical priesthood is in Christ, and in a more eminent manner; and whatever is wanting in those priests is in him. And no one taketh this honour — The priesthood. To himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron - And his posterity, who were all of them called at one and the same time. But it is observable, Aaron did not preach at all; preaching being no part of the priestly office.

So also Christ glorified not himself to be an high priest — That is, did not take this honour to himself, but received it from him who said, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee - Not, indeed, at the same time; for his generation was from eternity. Psalm ii, 7.
Psalm cx, 4.

The sum of the things treated of in the seventh and following chapters is contained, ver. 7-10; and in this sum is admirably comprised the process of his passion, with its inmost causes, in the very terms used by the evangelists. Who in the days of his flesh — Those two days, in particular, wherein his sufferings were at the height. Having offered up prayers and supplications - Thrice. With strong crying and tears - In the garden. To him that was able to save him from death - Which yet he endured, in obedience to the will of his Father. And being heard in that which he particularly feared - When the cup was offered him first, there was set before him that horrible image of a painful, shameful, accursed death, which moved him to pray conditionally against it: for, if he had desired it, his heavenly Father would have sent him more than twelve legions of angels to have delivered him. But what he most exceedingly feared was the weight of infinite justice; the being "bruised" and "put to grief" by the hand of God himself. Compared with this, everything else was a mere nothing; and yet, so greatly did he ever thirst to be obedient to the righteous will of his Father, and to "lay down" even "his life for the sheep," that he vehemently longed to be baptized with this baptism, Luke xii, 50. Indeed, his human nature needed the support of Omnipotence; and for this he sent up strong crying and tears: but, throughout his whole life, he showed that it was not the sufferings he was to undergo, but the dishonour that sin had done to so holy a God, that grieved his spotless soul. The consideration of its being the will of God tempered his fear, and afterwards swallowed it up; and he was heard not so that the cup should pass away, but so that he drank it without any fear.

Though he were a Son — This is interposed. lest any should be offended at all these instances of human weakness. In the garden, how frequently did he call God his Father! Matt. xxvi, 39, &c. And hence it most evidently appears that his being the Son of God did not arise merely from his resurrection. Yet learned he - The word learned, premised to the word suffered, elegantly shows how willingly he learned. He learned obedience, when be began to suffer; when he applied himself to drink that cup: obedience in suffering and dying.

And being perfected — By sufferings, chap. ii, 10; brought through all to glory. He became the author - The procuring and efficient cause. Of eternal salvation to all that obey him - By doing and suffering his whole will.

Called — The Greek word here properly signifies surnamed. His name is, "the Son of God." The Holy Ghost seems to have concealed who Melchisedec was, on purpose that he might be the more eminent type of Christ. This only we know, - that he was a priest, and king of Salem, or Jerusalem.

glossa.text: *For every high priest.* Because spiritual things do not so bring in the weak: as bodily things; from these he begins, wishing to show that the New Testament is better than the Old. But some things he sets down as common to Christ with the priests, some higher, pertaining to Christ alone. Some, further, more lowly, suiting those priests only.
*For that he himself also.* Take away here the occasion of exalting oneself above others.
*Neither doth any man,* etc. He strikes the covetous, who are not called, but thrust themselves forward.

*He did not glorify himself.* The Son was glorified by the Father, when he said: *This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased ((Matth. III))*. Which glorification was foretold long before through the Prophet: *Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee ((Psal. II))*.

*Thou art a priest.* Now Christ is a priest, not according to that whereby he was born of the Father, God with God, coeternal with him that begat him: but on account of the flesh consumed, on account of the victim which he offered for us. *According to the order of Melchisedech,* who was not temporal, Scripture keeping silence as to the beginning and the end of his life, in a figure of Christ who lacks beginning and end. And as he offered in bread and wine and once, so also Christ under the species of bread and wine gave his body and his blood to the disciples.

*Prayers and supplications.* He speaks of the action and the life of Christ, whose every action is the instruction of the faithful, and a prayer to God. Whatever Christ did, they were prayers and supplications for all. The shedding of his blood was a mighty cry, in which he was heard, for the reverence of that same passion. The reverence is this, that being without sin he suffered for charity alone. *He was heard.* By this it is plain that through him we can obtain mercy, since he is now at the right hand of the Father.
*He learned,* etc. That is, he willingly took upon himself obedience even unto death.

*To all that obey him.* So greatly does the passion avail, that it suffices for all unto salvation, which salvation can well be through him, because he himself *is called,* etc. *He was made the cause of salvation,* not of any sort of salvation, but of eternal; nor to few, but to all; yet on this condition, that they obey him. For otherwise they will not be able to obtain salvation. And he himself can well be the cause of salvation to the rest, since *he was called by God a high priest,* as he also himself showed in very deed by his works that he was such. For because he fulfilled the office of a high priest, and was obedient to the Father in all things, and in himself came to so great a consummation of all good things that it sufficed even for the salvation of others, therefore *he was called by God a high priest,* and this, *according to the order of Melchisedech,* namely, that all the order of divinity might be considered in him which could be considered in Melchisedech.

notes.text: Saying — By their mother. It was she, not they that uttered the words. Matt. xx, 20.

Ye know not what ye ask — Ye know not that ye ask for sufferings, which must needs pave the way to glory. The cup - Of inward; the baptism - Of outward sufferings. Our Lord was filled with sufferings within, and covered with them without.

Save to them for whom it is prepared — Them who by patient continuance in well doing, seek for glory, and honour, and immortality. For these only eternal life is prepared. To these, only he will give it in that day; and to every man his own reward, according to his own labour.
A ransom for many — Even for as many souls as needed such a ransom, 2 Cor. v, 15.

glossa.text: *And they come.* Having heard of the resurrection, forgetful of the second coming, they think that he will reign after the manner of men. Matthew says that the mother made the request, but Mark says that they themselves did, wishing to lay open the desire of those by whose counsel the mother asked.
*Or with the baptism.* The same as the cup. Whence elsewhere he says of his passion: *I have a baptism wherewith to be baptized: and how am I straitened until it be accomplished.*

*The cup indeed. ((BED.))* James is beheaded by Herod, John is cast into a cauldron of boiling oil. Thence the athlete of Christ went forth to the crown of martyrdom, and was at once banished to Patmos. And so he both was not wanting to martyrdom in mind, and drank the cup of confession which the three children drank in the furnace, although the persecutor did not shed his blood.

*But to sit.* As if to say, Do you wish that I should grant this to you? But the kingdom of heaven is not the giver's but the receiver's. *For there is no respect of persons with God ((Act. X))*, but whosoever shall be worthy shall receive that which is prepared not for the person but for the life. *To you.* Still proud, as if he said: If you wish to receive, be not what you are: it is prepared for others, and be you others, and it is prepared for you, which is, be humbled first, you who already wish to be exalted.
*They were indignant.* Not about the mother, but about the sons, who, not knowing their own measure, burned with immoderate greed.

*But Jesus calling them.* A humble master, and kind and gentle, he neither reproves the two for immoderate greed nor rebukes the ten for indignation and spite, but teaches that he is the greater who shall have been the less, and lord who is servant. In vain therefore do either those sigh after greater things or these grieve over their desire, since not power but humility leads to the summit of the virtues. Lastly he sets before his own an example, that if they made light of words, they might blush at deeds. *For the Son of man also, etc.*

echoes.text: “Bring Aaron your brother, and his sons with him, near to you from among the children of Israel, that he may minister to me in the priest’s office, even Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron’s sons.
echoes.note: ‘He is called by God, just like Aaron’ (v. 4) names Aaron's installation directly; Exod 28:1 is the foundational text where God ‘brings near’ Aaron to the priesthood. Moderate verbal volume (the proper name Aaron is shared) plus high thematic coherence with the high-priest argument seeded since 2:17 (Hays' recurrence).

echoes.text: to be a memorial to the children of Israel, to the end that no stranger, who isn’t of the offspring of Aaron, would come near to burn incense before Yahweh, that he not be as Korah, and as his company; as Yahweh spoke to him by Moses.
echoes.note: ‘Nobody takes this honor on himself’ (v. 4) recalls the Korah rebellion (Num 16–17), the locus classicus for seizing priesthood uninvited; the bronze-censer memorial of 16:40 warns against the ‘stranger’ who presumes. No verbatim quotation — a thematic allusion to the negative type behind Hebrews' rule of divine calling.

echoes.text: Moses said to Aaron, “Draw near to the altar, and offer your sin offering, and your burnt offering, and make atonement for yourself, and for the people; and offer the offering of the people, and make atonement for them; as Yahweh commanded.”
echoes.note: ‘He must offer sacrifices for sins for the people, as well as for himself’ (v. 3) compresses the cultic logic of Lev 9:7, where Aaron atones first ‘for yourself’ then ‘for the people.’ Verbal coherence (the doubled for-himself/for-the-people structure) marks this as the underlying script; the divergence Hebrews exploits is that Christ, sinless (4:15; 7:27), needs no offering for himself.

echoes.text: “Aaron shall offer the bull of the sin offering, which is for himself, and make atonement for himself and for his house.
echoes.note: The Day-of-Atonement requirement that the high priest atone ‘for himself’ (Lev 16:6) undergirds v. 3 and is the foil Hebrews overturns at 7:27. A faint echo paralleling Lev 9:7; recurrence of the Lev 16 figure already running through the letter (1:3; 9:7) raises its credence (Hays).

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, ‘You are my son. Today I have become your father.’
echoes.note: Re-cited from 1:5, now welded to priesthood: the same divine ‘today’ that enthrones the Son also installs him as high priest. Recurrence binding the two halves of the letter together.

echoes.text: Yahweh has sworn, and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.’
echoes.note: The hinge of the whole letter. Ps 110:1 crowned the Son at 1:13; now verse 4 of the same psalm makes him priest — a priesthood older than Aaron's, sworn by an oath. Named here, expounded at length in chapter 7.

echoes.text: Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine: and he was priest of God Most High.
echoes.note: The name ‘Melchizedek’ (vv. 6, 10) points beyond Ps 110:4 to its narrative root in Gen 14:18, the only other Old Testament Melchizedek text and the one ch. 7 will expound at length. The repeated naming is Hays' recurrence in advance — the figure is planted here and harvested in chapter 7.

echoes.text: For he has not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted, Neither has he hidden his face from him; but when he cried to him, he heard.
echoes.note: ‘Strong crying… having been heard for his godly fear’ (v. 7) reads the righteous sufferer's vindication: the very psalm of the cross (Ps 22, already cited at 2:12) testifies that God ‘heard’ the afflicted one's cry. Thematic coherence and recurrence of Ps 22 in Hebrews make this a heard, if unquoted, link to the Passion.

echoes.text: I love Yahweh, because he listens to my voice, and my cries for mercy. Because he has turned his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live. The cords of death surrounded me, the pains of Sheol got a hold of me. I found trouble and sorrow. Then I called on Yahweh’s name: “Yahweh, I beg you, deliver my soul.”
echoes.note: ‘Prayers and petitions… to him who was able to save him from death, and having been heard’ (v. 7) closely tracks the lament-deliverance pattern of Ps 116: encircled by the ‘cords of death,’ the petitioner cries and is heard. Scholars (Beale & Carson) hear the Gethsemane prayer voiced through the lament psalms; medium volume, strong thematic fit.

echoes.text: “Hear my prayer, Yahweh, and give ear to my cry. Don’t be silent at my tears. For I am a stranger with you, a foreigner, as all my fathers were.
echoes.note: ‘With strong crying and tears’ (v. 7) — the explicit ‘tears’ — faintly echoes the lament topos of Ps 39:12, where the sufferer begs God not to ‘be silent at my tears.’ Low verbal volume and a contested identification (any lament psalm could supply the motif), included for maximal coverage.

echoes.text: You shall not go out from the door of the Tent of Meeting for seven days, until the days of your consecration are fulfilled: for he shall consecrate you seven days.
echoes.note: ‘Having been made perfect’ (teleiōtheis, v. 9) carries the cultic sense of priestly ‘perfecting/consecration’ — the LXX teleioō word-group renders the ‘fill the hand’ ordination of Lev 8 (cf. 8:33, the seven-day consecration). A faint figural link: Christ's perfecting through suffering reworks the priest's installation rite. LXX-specific; invisible in the Hebrew ‘fill the hands.’

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand. After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall […]
echoes.note: The Servant who 'pours out his soul to death,' 'bears the sin of many,' and makes his life a guilt offering 'for many' is the controlling source for 'to give his life as a ransom for many.' The distinctive vicarious 'for many' (rabbim) and the substitutionary death match decisively. This is the chapter's major Servant allusion, high in Volume and Coherence.

echoes.text: Awake, awake, stand up, Jerusalem, that have drunk at the hand of Yahweh the cup of his wrath; you have drunken the bowl of the cup of staggering, and drained it.
echoes.note: Jerusalem has drunk 'the cup of his wrath... the bowl of staggering,' the cup-of-judgment imagery behind 'the cup that I drink.' Jesus takes upon himself the cup of divine wrath the city must drink. The cup as wrath to be consumed coheres with the passion's substitutionary logic.

echoes.text: For in the hand of Yahweh there is a cup, full of foaming wine mixed with spices. He pours it out. Indeed the wicked of the earth drink and drink it to its very dregs.
echoes.note: 'In the hand of the LORD there is a cup... and he pours it out; surely all the wicked of the earth shall drain it' establishes the cup as the draught of God's judgment. Jesus' question 'are you able to drink the cup that I drink' draws on this judicial cup. The wrath-cup motif's Recurrence (Jeremiah 25, Isaiah 51) supports it.

echoes.text: For thus says Yahweh, the God of Israel, to me: take this cup of the wine of wrath at my hand, and cause all the nations, to whom I send you, to drink it. They shall drink, and reel back and forth, and be mad, because of the sword that I will send among them. Then took I the cup at Yahweh’s hand, and made all the nations to drink, to whom Yahweh had sent me: Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, and its kings, and its princes, to make them a desolation, an […]
echoes.note: The prophet makes the nations drink 'the cup of the wine of wrath,' the most extended OT development of the wrath-cup that Jesus alludes to. It strengthens the Recurrence of the cup-of-judgment tradition behind Mark 10:38. Marked contested only as to which cup-text is primary; Isaiah 51 and Psalm 75 are nearer.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: James and John request seats 'in your glory,' echoing the dominion and glory given to the son of man, while the right-and-left thrones evoke enthronement in the Danielic kingdom. The petition presupposes the Son of Man's coming glory. Coherence with the Daniel 7 background of Mark's Son of Man title supports the link.

echoes.text: Yahweh says to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool for your feet.”
echoes.note: The request to sit 'at your right hand' draws on the royal enthronement of the king at God's right hand. The right-hand seat of honor is the Psalm 110 image Mark elsewhere applies to Jesus. The single-side request makes the echo partial but apt; marked contested as to directness.

echoes.text: The kingdom and the dominion, and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole sky, shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High: his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.
echoes.note: Dominion is given to the saints, yet the kingdom's authority is from God, against which the Gentile kings who 'lord it over' their nations are contrasted. Jesus' antithesis between Gentile rulers' domination and servanthood draws on this kingdom-of-God-versus-beastly-empires schema. The contrast of empires coheres with Daniel 7.

echoes.text: Seventy weeks are decreed on your people and on your holy city, to finish disobedience, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most holy. Know therefore and discern, that from the going out of the commandment to restore and to build Jerusalem to the Anointed One, the prince, shall be seven weeks, and sixty-two weeks: it shall be […]
echoes.note: The 'anointed one' cut off and atonement made 'for iniquity' resonates faintly with the ransoming death 'for many.' It supplies a Second-Temple frame for a representative figure's atoning death. Low and contested: conceptual, no verbal lock.

echoes.text: “When you take a census of the children of Israel, according to those who are numbered among them, then each man shall give a ransom for his soul to Yahweh, when you number them; that there be no plague among them when you number them.
echoes.note: The atonement-money 'ransom for his life' paid at the census supplies cultic background for lytron, 'ransom.' It frames a life-price offered to redeem. Contested and low: Mark's ransom is more directly Isaianic (53:10-12), but the redemption-price vocabulary is available here.

echoes.text: after he is sold he may be redeemed. One of his brothers may redeem him; or his uncle, or his uncle’s son, may redeem him, or any who is a close relative to him of his family may redeem him; or if he has grown rich, he may redeem himself.
echoes.note: The kinsman-redeemer who pays a price to redeem (gaal/lytron) supplies the OT economy of ransom behind 'a ransom for many.' It contributes Availability for the redemption metaphor. Contested; background vocabulary rather than citation.

echoes.text: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough,
echoes.note: No one can 'ransom' a brother or give God 'the price of his life,' for the ransom of a soul is costly, sharpening the surprise that the Son of Man does give exactly such a ransom 'for many.' The psalm sets up the impossibility Jesus' death answers. Contested and low: an inverted thematic contact.
